newsitem.title: BURMA: No word from Suu Kyi as top aide still detained.
newsitem.headline: No word from Suu Kyi as top aide still detained.

text.p: A top aide to Burmese democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi was still being held in detention on Thursday against a backdrop of world condemnation against the ruling military government.

Kyi Maung, deputy chairman of Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) party and a close adviser to the Nobel Peace laureate, was picked up on Wednesday for his involvement in a student protest this week, a senior government official said on Thursday.
The whereabouts of 75-year-old Kyi Maung was not known. All the government official would say was that he was still being held.
Suu Kyi, released from six years of house arrest in July 1995, could not be reached for comment on Thursday, with access to her home and telephone still cut off.

The United States and Amnesty International called for the immediate release of Kyi Maung, who was in Rangoon's infamous Insein Prison from 1990 to 1995 for his role in democracy movement activities in Burma.
The government official told Reuters Suu Kyi was still free to leave her University Avenue residence. However, some diplomats said they had heard she was not permitted to go out.
The road blocks on University Avenue, used by the military to prevent Suu Kyi's weekend democracy gatherings outside her house, were up for the third day on Thursday.
The diplomats said they expected Kyi Maung's detention to be temporary and was a sign of the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council's (SLORC) nervousness about any unrest in Rangoon.
"I think it is a very fluid situation. It shows that the government needs to find a new equilibrium and it has not found it. Its unstable," said one diplomat.

Kyi Maung was detained for questioning on Wednesday after the SLORC said he had met two students involved in a rare sit-in demonstration by up to 1,000 students of the Yangon Institute of Technology (YIT) early the same day.
The protest, held at an intersection about two km (1.2 miles) from Suu Kyi's house, ended without any arrests after the students were asked to go home, the government official said.
The students staged the demonstration to protest against the military government and its handling of a recent scuffle involving students at a food stall.
A similar scuffle at a tea shop in 1988 sparked nationwide outrage against the military government, leading to pro-democracy street demonstrations that left thousands dead or in jail.

Witnesses said they saw some riot police and security trucks near the YIT campus late on Wednesday night, but they had gone by morning. "Things seem to have returned to normal. We didn't see any sign of demonstration last night," said one eyewitness who lives near the campus.
Meanwhile, the U.S. urged the military authorities to start a dialogue with the opposition on the country's future.

"That's a very disturbing scene to see a peaceful student demonstration turned into a situation where arrests are made (and) people are held without any kind of charge against them," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
"This reflects the brutality of the Burmese government."

Amnesty, the London-based human rights organisation, said Kyi Maung had done nothing more than call for peaceful political change. "His arrest is an outrage and he should be released immediately. This arrest is part of a relentless attempt by the Myanmar (Burmese) authorities to crush any peaceful dissent by whatever means," Amnesty said in a statement.
Separately, the European Parliament called for economic sanctions against Burma because of human rights abuses.
In a resolution on Wednesday, the parliament condemned the SLORC for "violations of human rights and fundamental freedoms being perpetrated against the Burmese people".
